room.title: Neurodivergent Workers and Visual Thinkers
room.description: How a visual thinker keeps long work and scattered commitments in sight, so nothing depends on remembering where it lives: chunked sections, re-entry notes, energy-based planning and a parking lot for stray ideas.

desks.title: Year 2 grant report — written in visible chunks
desks.description: A 5,000-word funder report broken into sections you can see, each with its energy level, its blocks left and a re-entry note, so every work session starts with looking rather than searching.
desks.brief:
## Year 2 grant report — written in visible chunks

**For** Tumble Creek Catchment Group's regional environment funder
**Due** @+9d · **Length** 5,000 words max · **Reviewer** Ama, field coordinator
**Working style** 25-minute blocks, one section per block, a re-entry note at every stop

### Why this desk exists
A long report is where the thread gets lost: the outline lives in one app, the figures in a spreadsheet, the feedback in an email, and every switch costs twenty minutes of finding my place again. Here the whole report is in view — sections, figures, open questions — so starting a block means looking, not searching.

### Definition of done
- All 8 sections drafted and inside their word targets
- Every figure checked against the field-day register
- Ama has read Outcomes before it goes

### Where it stands
4 of 8 sections drafted, 2,710 of 5,000 words. 9 focus blocks left, and 6 of them need high focus. **Next block is Outcomes** — the hardest section, so it is booked for a morning.

callout.title: Re-entry point: Outcomes, paragraph 3
callout.body: Survival rates are drafted. Next: rates by site, which the funder asked for last year. Ama's survey results land @+1d — leave that part until they do. Six of the nine blocks left need high focus, so they're booked for mornings.

chart.title: Focus blocks left, by energy needed

mindmap.title: What the funder needs to see

blocks.p: One line at the end of every block, so the next one starts in two minutes instead of twenty.

ul: @-3d — Background done, 440 words. Left a gap for the site map caption.
@-2d — Activities done. 14 field days; totals match the register.
@-1d — Volunteers done. Next: Outcomes, starting with survival rates.
@today — Outcomes: survival paragraph drafted, 310 words. Stopped at rates by site.
One section per block. Anything I notice elsewhere goes on the parking-lot sticky, not into the document.
High-focus sections in the morning, low-energy sections after lunch.
It's fine to stop mid-sentence — the log says where.

blocks.p: All 8 sections are drafted, every figure matches the field-day register, Tomás has confirmed the final spend and Ama has read Outcomes.

notes.title: Funder feedback on last year's report
notes.body:
What they asked for, so I don't have to dig through email again:

- Fewer adjectives, more numbers
- Survival rates by site, not one average
- Four photos with captions, not twelve without
- The budget narrative arrived late last year — send it with the report this time

The second and fourth points are why Outcomes and the budget narrative are the two to watch.

desks.title: Weekly reset — every open loop in one place
desks.description: End-of-week reset: everything promised across email, chat and meetings pulled onto one board, sorted by energy and time, so next week starts with a plan rather than a scramble.
desks.brief:
## Weekly reset — every open loop in one place

**Role** communications adviser, Harbourside Arts Trust
**When** last hour of the working week, 45 minutes · **Next reset** @+7d
**Rule** if it isn't on this desk, it isn't a commitment yet

### Why a reset
Commitments arrive everywhere — a chat thread, an aside at the end of a meeting, an email flagged and forgotten. Things that aren't in view tend to vanish, so once a week every open loop comes out of those places and onto one list, with an energy level and a time guess beside it.

### This week
- 13 loops captured from 5 places — meetings produced the most (4)
- 4 done or dropped. Dropping counts as a decision.
- 9 carried forward: 7.5 hours in total, 4.5 of them high focus
- The first three for next week are on the yellow sticky

### What keeps it working
Capture first, sort second, decide last. No doing during the reset — even a two-minute loop goes on the list.

callout.title: Three high-focus loops, three mornings
callout.body: The workshop run sheet, the newsletter feature and the case-study questions are 4.5 of the 7.5 hours carried. Each gets a protected morning; low-energy loops fill the gaps between meetings.

rows.loop: Reply to Jun about the conference abstract
Newsletter feature on the youth programme
Fix broken links on the events page

chart.title: Where this week's loops came from

children.label: Nadia: which angle for the feature?

blocks.p: Same steps in the same order every week, so the reset itself needs no decisions.

ol: Capture (15 min): sweep email flags, saved chat messages, meeting notes, the calendar and the notebook. Everything goes into the table — no sorting yet.
Sort (10 min): an energy level and a minutes guess for each loop. Guess; don't research.
Decide (10 min): next up, this week, later, done or dropped. Pick three for the start of next week.
Protect (5 min): block mornings in the calendar for every high-focus loop.
Close (5 min): clear the parking lot and write one line on how the week went.

blocks.p: Meeting asides turned into commitments before I'd decided anything. Next week: say I'll confirm from my desk, then put it here.

blocks.quote: A dropped loop is a decision, not a failure.

notes.title: Meeting asides that became loops
notes.body:
Four of this week's loops came from meetings — more than any other source:

- Workshop planning: venue walk-through (done) and the run sheet (2 h)
- Team meeting: update the stakeholder list (50 min)
- Comms catch-up: photo permissions for Lina (done)

Two of the four were finished inside the week. The run sheet is the one that would have slipped without this list.

stickies.title: First three
stickies.body:
1. Reply to Jun (15 min)
2. Review Kofi's deck (30 min)
3. Case-study questions (60 min, morning)

stickies.body:

stickies.title: Between calls
stickies.body: 10-minute buffer: stand up, water, write one line on what was agreed.
